## Introduction

In this assignment, we explore the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset
and develop multiple linear regression models to predict
daily bicycle rentals.

We begin by importing and exploring the data, then prepare
the data for modeling, fit three regression models, and
compare their predictive performance using RMSE.

## Reading in the Data

```{r}
# Load the packages needed for data manipulation and exploration
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(rsample)
library(cowplot)

# Read the locally saved Seoul Bike Sharing dataset
# Specify Latin1 encoding to handle special characters
bike_data <- read_csv(
  "data/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "Latin1")
)

# Examine the structure of the dataset
glimpse(bike_data)
```

With the data imported, we conducted a basic EDA, including the following:
* checked for missingness
* created some numerical and some graphical summaries
* did some data manipulations
  * Turn the character variables (Seasons, Holiday, and Functioning Day) into factors.
  * Lastly, rename the all the variables to have easy to use names

```{r}
missingValues <- colSums(is.na(bike_data))

# Histos
plot_A <- ggplot(data = bike_data, aes(x = `Temperature(°C)`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "red3", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Temperatures", x = "Temperature", y = "Count")

plot_B <- ggplot(data = bike_data, aes(x = `Humidity(%)`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Temperatures", x = "Humidity", y = "Count")

# Simple Bar Graph
plot_C <- ggplot(data = bike_data, aes(x = Seasons)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "red3", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Number of Rides by Season", x = "Season", y = "Number of Rides")

plotsABC <- plot_grid(plot_A, plot_B, plot_C, labels = c("A", "B", "C"), ncol = 3)

clean_bikes <- bike_data |>
  mutate(
    #Fix current vars:
    Date = dmy(Date)
  ) |>
  # Convert string to a true date obj.
  rename(
    date          = Date,
    bike_count    = `Rented Bike Count`, # Note the backticks for spaces!
    hour          = Hour,
    temperature   = `Temperature(°C)`,
    humidity      = `Humidity(%)`,
    wind_speed    = `Wind speed (m/s)`,
    visibility    = `Visibility (10m)`,         
    dewPoint      = `Dew point temperature(°C)`,
    solarRadiation= `Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)`,
    rainfall      = `Rainfall(mm)`,
    snowfall      = `Snowfall (cm)`,
    season        = Seasons,
    holiday       = Holiday,
    functDay      = `Functioning Day`
  ) |>
  # Make New vars:
  mutate(
    dayOfWeek = wday(date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE), # Extract day name (Mon, etc.)
      dayOfWeek = factor(dayOfWeek, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")),
    isWeekend = if_else(dayOfWeek %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"), 1, 0), #dummy
    isWeekend = as.factor(isWeekend),
    month = month(date, label = TRUE), # Extract monht.
      month = factor(month, levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")),
    monthNumber = month(date), #Month number, for slightly off "season" trend analyiss.
    monthNumber = as.factor(monthNumber)
  )

#Create output
newVars <- clean_bikes |> select(dayOfWeek:monthNumber) |> lapply(table)

myList <- list(missingValues, plotsABC, newVars)
myList
```

There do not appear to be any missing variables, and season appears mostly uniform. We created some variables to help look at larger trends (months) and smaller trends (weekdays vs. weekends) in later analysis.

Then we summarized across the hours so that each day had one observation and value for all categorical/factor variables, and shows:
• sum of the bike_count, rainfall, and snowfall variables
• mean of all the other weather related variables.


```{r}
compressed_bikes <- clean_bikes |>
  group_by(date, season, holiday) |>
  summarize(
    across(c(bike_count, rainfall, snowfall), sum, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(c(temperature, humidity, wind_speed, visibility, dewPoint, solarRadiation), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    across(dayOfWeek:monthNumber, first),
  )
```
Then we recreated our basic summary stats and then create some plots to explore relationships.
